Not every dog can do this, and not every trainer can or should. With the owners' permission, I used Bishop to help communicate a lesson to Ryder. Dogs naturally understand other dogs better than they understand us. The goal wasn't to make Ryder love every dog she sees-it was to teach her that she doesn't need to react to every dog she sees. Before training, a simple neighborhood walk was nearly impossible. Seeing another dog meant lunging, pulling, and trying to start conflict. Through obedience work and carefully controlled sessions with Bishop, Ryder learned a valuable lesson: not every dog is a threat, and not every situation requires a reaction. Also notice how Bishop's corrections increase in intensity throughout the video. He starts with the minimum amount of pressure necessary and only escalates when Ryder chooses not to listen. That's how dogs naturally communicate with one another. Will I tell these owners to take her to a dog park and expect her to be everyone's best friend? Absolutely not. But can we give her a better quality of life by helping her calmly walk past another dog across the street? Absolutely. Not every dog needs this type of training, but some dogs can benefit tremendously from it. It’s no secret that my time in medicine almost killed me. - And I think the biggest reason why (more than the hours and the exhaustion) was this idea that we’re supposed to accept all of it with a smile. With gratitude. As if the system is doing us a FAVOUR. The 14-hour shifts, 7 days in a row. The mental overwhelm from having urgent 7 tasks competing for your attention. The constant anxiety and fear of making the wrong mistake that could cost a life. The superiors who look straight through you. And then, when you say anything about it, you’re met with: “Oh but how LUCKY are you to be a doctor?” “You’re saving lives, why would you want to do anything else?” That’s the part that really f*cking broke me 😞 I ended up leaving medicine because I just couldn’t take it any longer. And even then, I felt so guilty because of this exact attitude. I thought I was weak, for choosing not to suffer for such a prestigious career. But now that I’ve built a career that I genuinely LOVE and ENJOY every single day… I’ve learnt that suffering SHOULDN’T be a rite of passage. It’s not what makes you a good doctor. It’s not what makes you “worthy” of the title. And it was NEVER supposed to be the price you pay for a career that you love. The more that we say this out loud, and support others who are brave enough to say it too, the louder that calling gets. So, are you with me? 🙏🏽 - P.S.
